routes.description: Establish Christian theism as the better account of reality through a cumulative comparison involving biological information and organization, cosmic features, resurrection testimony, and the compatibility of divine goodness with nonbelief, religious geography, and suffering.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its positive design and resurrection inferences jointly favor Christian theism over naturalism and its explanations of hiddenness and suffering prevent the principal naturalistic counterevidence from reversing that comparison.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined positive evidence and answers to counterevidence make the observed reality more expected under Christian theism than under atheistic naturalism.

centralBridges.description: Connect biological information, genetic-code optimization, and interdependent replication systems to intelligent causation rather than unguided naturalistic origins.
Establish that the testimonial and historical data are better explained by Jesus's resurrection than by deception, mistake, development, hallucination, or other naturalistic alternatives.
Explain sincere nonbelief and uneven religious access consistently with divine love, adequate evidence, moral probation, proportionate judgment, and mercy.
Limit the disconfirming force of human and animal suffering by identifying relevant goods, evidential dependencies, epistemic limits, or features of an orderly world.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend likelihood-based and positive-causal inference as appropriate methods for comparing theism and naturalism without treating every unresolved mechanism as decisive.
Use cosmic beginning, fine-tuning, religious history, or public corroboration as supporting considerations within the cumulative comparison.

routes.description: Establish atheistic naturalism as the better account by challenging design and resurrection inferences, explaining religious belief and experience naturalistically, and treating sincere nonbelief, religious geography, and apparently gratuitous suffering as evidence against Christian theism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic explanations or warranted uncertainty undercut the principal positive arguments for Christian theism while hiddenness, culturally patterned religion, and suffering remain more expected under naturalism.

motionBridge.description: Show that naturalistic explanations plus the comparative counterevidence account for the observed reality better than Christian theism does.

centralBridges.description: Show that unresolved biological origins or complexity do not warrant intelligent design and remain appropriately addressed through natural mechanisms, scientific development, or suspended judgment.
Show that textual development, uncertain testimony, neurological or psychological experiences, and ordinary historical explanations remain preferable to a resurrection inference.
Establish that sincere nonbelief and culturally patterned religious distribution are expected under naturalism but conflict with an adequately revealing and perfectly loving God.
Establish that apparently purposeless human and animal suffering is more expected under naturalism and is not adequately explained by stable laws, unknown divine reasons, or human-centered goods.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require positive comparative support before moving from gaps in current naturalistic knowledge to supernatural or specifically Christian conclusions.
Explain religious belief and consoling narratives through cultural, psychological, or neurological processes that do not presuppose their truth.

sections.title: Biological information, organization, and naturalistic origins
sections.rationale: The affirmative's principal design case rests on DNA and RNA information, genetic-code optimization, replication, and irreducible complexity, while the opposing burden is to test whether these support intelligence or merely expose unresolved natural history.

sections.title: Resurrection testimony and naturalistic alternatives
sections.rationale: The resurrection case is the principal route from general theistic possibility to specifically Christian theism, making testimonial reliability, Gospel development, apostolic conduct, prior probability, and alternative experiences central to the motion.

sections.title: Divine hiddenness, sincere nonbelief, and religious geography
sections.rationale: Nonresistant nonbelief and geographically uneven religion directly compare what a loving revelatory God and a culturally mediated naturalistic world would lead observers to expect.

sections.title: Human and animal suffering under theism and naturalism
sections.rationale: Apparently gratuitous, minor, and animal suffering supplies a major comparative challenge to divine goodness, while theistic replies invoke orderly laws, possible goods, evidential dependence, and limits on human access to reasons.

sections.title: Comparative inference, religious experience, and worldview explanation
sections.rationale: The debate repeatedly disputes when likelihoods, scientific track records, causal analogies, supernatural mechanisms, and naturalistic genealogies of religious belief legitimately shift the comparison between the worldviews.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: Digitally encoded information in DNA and RNA is more plausibly explained by an intelligent conscious cause than by naturalism.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces McLatchie, and the uninterrupted opening statement explicitly presents this as his biological-information argument.

response.rationale: This is a constructive biological-design inference and therefore has no earlier opposing target; its responsiveness is assessed within the constructive class.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly advances a principal affirmative route through an explicit causal analogy, though the alternative comparison is compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is recoverable as a best-explanation claim, with intelligence, information, DNA, and RNA used consistently.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The phrase best explanation appropriately signals comparison, but the habitual association cited does not fully establish the biological probability claim.

charity.alternative: Natural processes can generate biologically functional sequence patterns without conscious agency.
charity.decisiveQualification: The analogy requires relevant similarity between human symbolic products and biochemical information, not merely shared informational vocabulary.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogical inference is intelligible, but the bridge from familiar symbolic artifacts to molecular sequences remains materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt supplies examples of designed information but offers little representative biological evidence or comparative testing of natural alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, this directly supplies the core intelligent-causation step for the biological-design bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies intelligent production as a rival but does not seriously develop the strongest natural-process alternative or the decisive analogy qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source expressly compares DNA and RNA information with hieroglyphs, headlines, and programming, then attributes it to an intelligent conscious cause.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: The genetic code's error-minimizing optimization and resistance to gradual reassignment support design over an evolutionary naturalistic origin.
moves.attributionBasis: McLatchie's continuous opening statement explicitly introduces the genetic code and develops the optimization and evolvability claims in his own voice.

response.rationale: This is a constructive optimization and evolvability argument with no earlier opposing target; responsiveness is assessed only within its constructive class.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It develops a distinct empirical-looking reason for the main design route, although the final design comparison is not fully defended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The genetic-code reassignment claim is clear and stable, while the limits of the catastrophic-effect generalization remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical resistance-to-evolution conclusion exceeds the excerpt's support because feasible historical pathways and rival models are not compared.

charity.alternative: Code evolution could occur before modern cellular dependencies became fixed or through limited reassignment mechanisms.
charity.decisiveQualification: Present-day costs of global reassignment do not by themselves show that earlier code formation or constrained evolution was impossible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from disruptive reassignment to limited current evolvability is coherent, but the further bridge to design remains underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The asserted cellular consequences are specific, yet no representative optimization evidence, measurements, or serious evolutionary comparison is provided here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The argument directly addresses whether genetic-code structure and optimization complete a major step in the biological-design route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move stresses catastrophic contemporary reassignment but omits the strongest historical-development qualification, materially weakening the naturalistic alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source argues that changing codon assignments would alter every produced polypeptide and wreak havoc, using this constraint to resist an evolutionary account.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: The apostles' costly perseverance and the Gospel use of women as tomb witnesses make deliberate fabrication of the resurrection claims improbable.
moves.attributionBasis: McLatchie introduces the resurrection itself and develops both considerations as reasons against deception in his own continuous presentation.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies considerations against deliberate fabrication and has no earlier opposing target; responsiveness is assessed within the constructive class.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly develops a major resurrection alternative test through costly perseverance and witness-selection considerations, despite documentation gaps.

precisionFindings.rationale: The anti-fabrication conclusion is clear, but the scope of apostolic hardship, martyrdom, and responsibility for Gospel details is not fully delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling deception enormously improbable overstates what costly sincerity and a literary witness detail establish without independent historical verification.

charity.alternative: Sincere later perseverance and women in a narrative can coexist with exaggeration, legend, or fabrication by other transmitters.
charity.decisiveQualification: Evidence of some adherents' sincerity does not identify every claimant or establish that the relevant reports originated with those who suffered.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Costly perseverance reasonably bears on sincerity, but the inference bundles disputed authorship and transmission premises without completing those bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific considerations are named, yet the identities, fates, independence, and provenance needed to warrant them are largely asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Testing deliberate deception directly advances the indispensable resurrection bridge and is near the top of the central relevance tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move engages lying as an alternative but omits the decisive separation between sincerity, authorship, transmission, and the truth of particular reports.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites apostolic dangers, persecution, suffering, and martyrdom, and the locked proposition also records the appeal to women as tomb witnesses.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: Extended, varied, physical, and group encounters reported with the risen Jesus make honest perceptual mistake an improbable explanation of the testimony.
moves.attributionBasis: McLatchie marks this as his second testimonial consideration and immediately concludes that the evidence favors Jesus having risen from the dead.

response.rationale: This is a constructive argument against honest perceptual mistake and has no earlier opposing target; responsiveness is evaluated within the constructive class.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly addresses a major naturalistic alternative with varied alleged encounter features, though it assumes the reports' historical reliability.

precisionFindings.rationale: The anti-mistake thesis is recoverable, but the scope shifts from what texts report to what encounters actually occurred without explicit qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The force would fit verified encounters, but the move does not acknowledge that the testimonial descriptions themselves require historical defense.

charity.alternative: Visionary experiences, memory development, and later narrative elaboration could jointly produce varied physical and group reports.
charity.decisiveQualification: Refuting a simple individual hallucination does not eliminate composite naturalistic accounts involving textual and social development.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The encounter features would count against simple individual error, but the inference presupposes rather than establishes their historical occurrence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several concrete reported features are listed, yet their source independence, dating, corroboration, and reliability are not defended in the move.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly tests perceptual mistake, an indispensable alternative within the central resurrection bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly identifies mistake as a rival but treats it too narrowly and omits the strongest composite-development qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source lists individual and group sightings, conversations, long discourses, physical contact, meals, and appearances extended over forty days.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Non-resistant nonbelief conflicts with the existence of a perfectly loving God who would remain open to relationship, thereby supporting atheism over Christian theism.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the floor to O'Connor, who announces divine hiddenness as his first argument and formally states its premises and conclusion.

response.rationale: This constructive hiddenness argument has no earlier opposing target; it is evaluated for how well it develops the naturalistic route within the constructive class.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It formally states the decisive premises and directly connects nonresistant nonbelief to the conflict with perfect divine love.

precisionFindings.rationale: The premises, perfect-love condition, occurrence claim, and atheistic conclusion are stated in a stable and readily recoverable form.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The deductive force follows from the stated premises, but the necessary link between perfect love and constant relational availability needs further defense.

charity.alternative: A loving God may permit temporary nonbelief for morally sufficient goods while remaining ultimately open to relationship.
charity.decisiveQualification: Any such good must explain genuinely nonresistant seekers without making divine love or relational openness merely nominal.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The formal inference is valid given its premises, with one bounded but important bridge linking perfect love to absence of nonresistant nonbelief.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The occurrence of sincere open nonbelief is asserted plausibly and specifically, but representative evidence and rival explanations are not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This directly supplies the core incompatibility claim for the central hiddenness-and-geography bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move frames the love-based demand fairly, though it does not fully explore temporary hiddenness or morally sufficient divine reasons.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source gives a numbered argument that perfect love excludes nonresistant nonbelief, asserts that such nonbelief occurs, and concludes that no perfectly loving God exists.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The geographic concentration of theistic belief is better explained by culturally produced religion than by a universally loving God who is comparably accessible to people everywhere.
moves.attributionBasis: The continuous opening statement, direct address to Jonathan, and naturalist conclusion clearly establish O'Connor's authorship.

response.rationale: This constructive geographical argument has no earlier opposing target; responsiveness is assessed within the constructive class for the naturalistic route.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies a direct comparative observation and explicitly asks which worldview better explains the geographic distribution of belief.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative proposition is clear, but the referenced geographic concentration and populations are only partly specified in the selected evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move uses comparative likelihood language rather than certainty, and the stated cultural dependence supports that limited evidential force.

charity.alternative: Uneven belief could reflect differing human resistance, historical missions, or providentially varied access rather than God's absence.
charity.decisiveQualification: The theistic alternative must explain why birthplace so strongly predicts belief without unsupported population-level differences in resistance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative inference is coherent and explicit, though it leaves an implicit bridge from geographical correlation to cultural causation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A striking claimed geographic disparity is identified, but the excerpt does not document its measurement, representativeness, or relevant confounders.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The observation directly advances the central burden of showing culturally patterned religion to be more expected under naturalism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move squarely considers differential resistance as a theistic explanation and identifies its substantial comparative cost.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source says the likelihood of theism is intimately tied to birthplace and contrasts cultural production with a hypothesis of large population differences in resistance.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Apparently gratuitous suffering is evidence against an all-loving and powerful God because even one genuinely unnecessary instance would lack the purpose required by standard theistic explanations.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly introduces his third fact and develops it within O'Connor's uninterrupted opening statement.

response.rationale: This constructive suffering argument has no earlier opposing target; its responsiveness is assessed within the constructive class for the naturalistic route.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly states the decisive evidential condition and relates it to familiar theistic purposes such as freedom and character formation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between apparently and actually unnecessary suffering is maintained, and the one-instance condition is explicitly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move cautiously relies on apparent cases and conditions its conclusion on an actual unnecessary instance, fitting the stated warrant.

charity.alternative: Unknown goods or necessary connections could make apparently pointless suffering justified despite human inability to identify the purpose.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bare possibility of unknown reasons does not erase evidential force unless their likelihood and connection to the suffering are defended.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional argument is coherent and carefully separates appearance from actuality, with a bounded bridge concerning evidential appearance.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The framework is well stated, but the selected passage supplies intuition rather than a developed representative case or likelihood comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly establishes the main evidential framework for the central naturalistic suffering bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes several standard theistic purposes, though unknown-reason accounts receive only implicit treatment.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source considers freedom, moral development, and other divine ends, then argues that some suffering appears unable to serve them and conditions the argument on one actual case.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Animal suffering is more expected under naturalism and is especially difficult for theism because animals lack the freedom, moral development, and assured compensation invoked to explain human suffering.
moves.attributionBasis: The continuous opening turn explicitly introduces animals as a final consideration and closes with O'Connor's comparative conclusion.

response.rationale: This constructive animal-suffering argument has no earlier opposing target; responsiveness is assessed within the constructive class for the suffering route.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly compares worldview expectations and systematically tests several leading human-centered theodicies against animal suffering.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claims about freedom, moral development, and compensation are presented as targeted limitations, including an express most-accounts qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Animal suffering strongly burdens the listed defenses, but saying it is infinitely more difficult exceeds the comparative support supplied.

charity.alternative: Animal suffering could support ecological goods, stable natural laws, creaturely development, or eventual compensation.
charity.decisiveQualification: A successful account must explain the scale and distribution of suffering without relying only on goods peculiar to human moral agency.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The elimination of several human-centered explanations is cogent, though it does not establish that all relevant theistic explanations fail.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument uses specific structural differences between animals and humans, but offers little evidence about scale, cognition, or alternative goods.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Animal suffering is a principal and independently difficult component of the central naturalistic suffering bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move handles major human-centered defenses accurately but omits ecological, law-based, and nonhuman-good alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source argues animals lack the relevant freedom and moral development and, on most accounts, heavenly compensation, making standard human theodicies inapplicable.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: Divine hiddenness is compatible with Christianity because God may appropriately limit evidence while still providing adequate grounds to sincere inquirers.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces McLatchie's rebuttal, and the entire first-person response remains within his uninterrupted speaking turn.

components.text: Explain why a perfectly loving God may permit genuinely nonresistant nonbelief while remaining open to relationship.
Explain why sincere access to adequate evidence varies strongly with geographic and cultural location.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the love-and-hiddenness demand by proposing limited but adequate evidence and omnisciently informed restraint. It does not answer the independent geographic distribution demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer contacting the decisive nonresistant-nonbelief component while leaving the geographic component uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The thesis is recoverable, but adequate evidence and sincere inquirer are not operationalized, and the scope of the counterfactual claim is unclear.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reply offers a possible compatibility account and uses presumptive language, appropriately avoiding a claim that the divine rationale is demonstrated.

charity.alternative: A sincerely open person may remain unconvinced despite honestly engaging all evidence available to them.
charity.decisiveQualification: Appealing to what God knows the person would do with more evidence must not redefine observed nonresistance by an inaccessible counterfactual.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The compatibility story is possible, but it risks circular reliance on prior confidence in divine goodness and leaves the counterfactual principle unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reply mainly asserts powerful Christian evidence, scriptural goodness, and divine counterfactual knowledge without supplying verification in this move.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central hiddenness bridge by offering a reason for limiting evidence while claiming sincere seekers retain adequate grounds.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply acknowledges sincere inquiry but weakens the alternative by relying on unverifiable counterfactual rejection and trust in antecedent evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source invokes powerful evidence for Christianity, trust in God's goodness, and divine knowledge of whether additional evidence would produce relationship or rejection.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: The evidential force of suffering is limited by dependence among instances, convergent positive evidence for theism, and suffering's dependence on consciousness.
moves.attributionBasis: McLatchie explicitly transitions to the problem of evil and develops the response without any speaker change.

components.text: Show why apparently unnecessary suffering should not substantially disconfirm an all-loving and powerful God.
Explain animal suffering without relying only on freedom, human moral development, or assured compensation.

response.rationale: The reply directly limits the general evidential inference through dependence, positive evidence, and consciousness, but it does not contact the distinct animal-suffering demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer that contacts the decisive general evidential component while leaving the animal-specific challenge unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: Finite evidential value and comparative consciousness claims are clear, though the proposed dependence among suffering instances is not fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The finite-evidence conclusion is cautious, but the claim that consciousness is much more likely on theism is asserted more strongly than defended.

charity.alternative: Even dependent instances of suffering may collectively remain substantially more expected under naturalism than under theism.
charity.decisiveQualification: Finite evidential value does not imply weak evidential value, and positive theistic evidence must be independently warranted before offsetting it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The limiting considerations are relevant, but their relationship to the likelihood of suffering under each worldview remains only partly developed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The consciousness likelihood and dependence claims rely largely on assertion and named authority without a defended comparative warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply directly supports the central affirmative suffering bridge by attempting to limit the force of the opposing evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accepts evidential relevance but does not fully address the strongest likelihood comparison or the distinction between finite and small force.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source argues consciousness is more probable on theism, suffering surprises both views, and the problem of evil has finite evidential value.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: Minor suffering may be an unavoidable byproduct of a regular, intelligible world whose stable laws enable moral agency and scientific inquiry.
moves.attributionBasis: McLatchie explicitly takes up O'Connor's menial-suffering example and completes the response before closing his rebuttal.

components.text: Explain why apparently minor or unnecessary harms may nonetheless arise in a purposive world governed by a good God.
Explain the scale and distinctive moral difficulty of animal suffering under stable natural laws.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the minor-harm component by connecting occasional harm to stable intelligible laws and agency, but it leaves the animal-specific scale and distribution challenge unanswered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive minor-harm component is contacted, producing a substantial partial answer, while a distinct animal-suffering component remains uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is clearly limited to occasional harm and possible universes with regular scientifically intelligible laws.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reply carefully says it is unclear that an elegant lawful universe could avoid occasional harm, matching its modest modal support.

charity.alternative: Stable laws might permit far less harm, or God might intervene selectively without destroying regularity or inquiry.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing some harm may accompany regular laws does not establish the necessity, quantity, or distribution of actual suffering.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposed connection between stable laws, agency, inquiry, and occasional harm is coherent, though necessity is not demonstrated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The goods of regularity and science are identifiable, but the no-better-world modal premise is asserted without comparative support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier it materially supports the suffering bridge, but only for the narrower issue of occasional minor harm.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly identifies the value of regularity but does not fully address selective intervention or the scale qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source connects the moral arena and scientific inquiry with a regular, predictable, intelligible world and questions whether such a world can avoid occasional harm.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Present inability to explain DNA replication naturalistically does not warrant intelligent design, given science's history of explaining complexities previously claimed to require divine agency.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator gives O'Connor the rebuttal, and he explicitly addresses Jonathan's biological-complexity argument throughout this uninterrupted passage.

components.text: Supply a warranted bridge from unexplained biological information to intelligent conscious causation rather than mere present ignorance.
Show that genetic-code optimization and constraints positively favor design over possible natural historical development.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses the inference as moving from current lack of understanding to a claim that science cannot explain the system, and states that suspended inquiry rather than design follows.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly attacks the decisive inferential bridge shared by both biological-design moves and states the defeating epistemic consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between current ignorance, in-principle scientific limits, and a positive design conclusion is explicit and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The demand for suspension is well calibrated, though the appeal to science's history does not guarantee a future naturalistic explanation.

charity.alternative: The design argument may be a positive causal inference from specified features rather than an inference solely from ignorance.
charity.decisiveQualification: The criticism succeeds only to the extent that the affirmative has not established discriminating evidence for intelligence beyond naturalistic incompleteness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between unexplained and inexplicable is clear, and the conclusion of suspended inference follows unless positive design evidence is supplied.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Science's explanatory history is relevant but broadly invoked, with no representative cases or detailed engagement with the specific molecular evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply directly supplies the central naturalistic burden by attacking the main inference from unresolved biological complexity to design.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply engages the central gap concern fairly but somewhat compresses the affirmative's analogy and optimization claims into ignorance.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source says irreducible complexity leaves a lack of understanding and argues that design would require assuming secular investigation can never adequately explain DNA replication.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Absent an antecedent assumption that God exists, ordinary naturalistic explanations of resurrection reports remain more plausible than an actual resurrection, even if familiar alternatives have weaknesses.
moves.attributionBasis: The move occurs within Alex O'Connor's uninterrupted rebuttal turn and explicitly contrasts the naturalist's priors with the theistic resurrection hypothesis.

components.text: Show that an actual resurrection is comparatively better than ordinary or composite naturalistic explanations of the reported encounters.
Show that costly sincerity and women witnesses exclude ordinary transmission, embellishment, or deception sufficiently to favor resurrection.

response.rationale: The reply contacts both testimonial moves by shifting the comparison to antecedent worldview probability and maintaining that weaknesses in familiar alternatives do not establish resurrection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive comparative demand for both resurrection moves, though it gives little detailed alternative analysis.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional contrast between theistic and naturalistic priors is explicit, and the comparative conclusion is readily recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker allows that resurrection may be best conditional on theism while asserting only comparative naturalistic plausibility without that assumption.

charity.alternative: The testimonial likelihood ratio could overcome a low resurrection prior if the reports are sufficiently expected under resurrection and unlikely otherwise.
charity.decisiveQualification: Prior improbability alone is not decisive; the posterior comparison also requires likelihoods for the specific evidence under each hypothesis.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The prior-probability point is coherent, but the full posterior comparison is incomplete without likelihoods for the reported evidence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move asserts that ordinary explanations remain preferable but does not specify base rates or defend a particular naturalistic account.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central naturalistic resurrection bridge by reframing the comparison around antecedent worldview probability.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly grants the conditional theistic case but omits the decisive possibility that strong evidence could overcome a low prior.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source concedes resurrection might be the best explanation if God is assumed, while insisting the debate must compare explanations without assuming theism.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The increase in number and detail of resurrection appearances across progressively later Gospels supports a naturalistic account in which the tradition developed or was embellished over time.
moves.attributionBasis: The entire move is delivered by Alex O'Connor during the same rebuttal, with a continuous comparison of the Gospel appearance traditions.

components.text: Show whether the increasingly detailed physical and group appearance reports are early independent evidence or later narrative development.
Show whether Gospel witness details reliably originate with the apostles rather than developing in later textual transmission.

response.rationale: The reply contacts both resurrection moves by challenging the provenance of their testimonial details through an alleged chronological increase in appearances and elaboration.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly addresses the evidential status of the cited reports, though the textual chronology and source relationships are compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The development thesis is clear, but earliest Gospel, no resurrection, and increasing appearances conflate endings, appearances, and resurrection proclamation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The observed narrative pattern can support development, but the account omits qualifications about Mark's ending, source dependence, and earlier traditions.

charity.alternative: Later Gospels may preserve independent or earlier traditions, while Mark's shorter ending need not imply absence of resurrection belief.
charity.decisiveQualification: Literary dating and increasing detail do not alone determine when the underlying appearance traditions originated.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Increasing detail over time is relevant to embellishment, but the inference needs a bridge from document chronology to tradition chronology.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific Gospel comparisons are offered, yet textual dating, endings, source dependence, and earlier appearance traditions are insufficiently documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central naturalistic resurrection bridge by contesting the historical reliability of the affirmative's appearance evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move raises a serious development hypothesis but omits the decisive distinction between a text's date and its traditions' dates.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source contrasts Mark, Matthew, Luke, and John and argues that later texts contain more and more detailed appearances, including Emmaus and Thomas.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: Some divine hiddenness is necessary for earthly life to function as a probationary arena for genuine moral character formation.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer follows O'Connor's direct question, and the first-person references to the opening and rebuttal identify McLatchie as the speaker.

components.text: Explain why perfect divine love permits some sincere people to lack belief and therefore lack an available divine relationship.
Explain why the amount of hiddenness and access to belief tracks geography and culture so unevenly.

response.rationale: The probationary-arena explanation contacts the general reason a loving God might remain less salient, but it does not explain geographic variation or fully address sincere relational openness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer contacting the principal hiddenness rationale while leaving the separate geographic distribution component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The moral-choice-arena proposition is recoverable and stable, though how much awareness would defeat probation is left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move says some hiddenness is necessary but does not establish why unmistakable awareness would prevent genuine moral choice or character formation.

charity.alternative: People can make genuine moral choices while knowing that authorities, loved ones, or God exist and care about their conduct.
charity.decisiveQualification: The probation account must show that divine awareness uniquely coerces virtue rather than merely informing morally significant choice.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A probationary purpose is compatible with some hiddenness, but the claimed necessity depends on an unsupported link between awareness and impaired agency.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The moral-choice model is asserted without evidence that divine salience would undermine rather than improve responsible character formation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central affirmative hiddenness bridge by offering a morally sufficient purpose for limited divine visibility.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses moral formation but omits the strongest objection that knowledge of an observer need not eliminate freedom or authentic character.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source describes earthly life as probation and a moral-choice arena in which people shape character, suggesting constant divine awareness would interfere.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Ignorance about abiogenesis and the intuitive appeal of a single origin of life do not support God unless they can be formulated as a nonfallacious argument rather than an inference from a gap.
moves.attributionBasis: The audience question is addressed to Alex, and the answer contrasts its admitted uncertainty with Jonathan's treatment of God-of-the-gaps reasoning.

components.text: Show that ignorance about life's origin provides positive discriminating evidence for intelligence rather than a gap-based inference.
Show that apparent uniqueness or code constraints establish design rather than warranting continued uncertainty about origins.

response.rationale: The reply expressly distinguishes admitted ignorance and intuitive appeal from a nonfallacious positive argument, concluding that God is unsupported until that inferential burden is met.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: Although the mechanism by which a supernatural realm interacts with matter may be unknowable, people can still possess sufficient justification for believing that such a realm exists.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the question to McLatchie, whose uninterrupted answer explicitly compares supernatural causation with mind-brain interaction.
